odeProperty.value: We continue our journey through the Baroque period.

odeComponent.htmlView:
The Baroque period was an era of extreme contrasts in which music, politics and art came together to impress and move society through three main themes:

  • Politics and Economy: absolutist monarchs and the high nobility concentrated all power in their hands and used art and grand courtly festivities as a propaganda tool to demonstrate their wealth and superiority.
  • Society and Religion: in a Europe in crisis, ravaged by wars and disease and divided between Catholics and Protestants, the Church and the rulers turned public life into a theatrical spectacle to stir the emotions of a population seeking refuge in religion and entertainment.
  • Art and Music: both in painting (with chiaroscuro) and in music (with shifts between loud and soft), the main aim was to break with the balance of the Renaissance through movement, excessive ornamentation, surprise and drama, giving rise to major musical genres such as opera.

New musical elements emerged that shaped the development of a new musical style very different from that of the Renaissance:

The new texture: melody and accompaniment

During the Baroque period, traditional polyphony was abandoned because it was considered too complex and confusing for the listener; instead, composers sought music that was clearer and more emotive. To solve this problem, Baroque composers developed the main texture into the melody and accompaniment: a single lead voice takes centre stage (and carries the text) very clearly, whilst the instruments provide a harmonic accompaniment in the background. This marked the birth of the modern concept of "singer + band" that we still use today.

The basso continuo

This is the accompaniment technique used in absolutely all Baroque music. It is the bass and percussion line of the period, the rhythmic and harmonic foundation upon which the main melody rests. It consists of two elements working together:

  • A low-pitched instrument that plays the bass line: usually a cello or a bassoon. It plays the lowest notes continuously.
  • An instrument capable of playing chords: usually the harpsichord, the organ or the lute. It enriches the sound by playing chords that complement the bass line.
Contrasts

Moving from a forte passage to a piano one, shifting from a soloist to the orchestra taking over… Baroque music is full of contrasts.

Regular pulse

The music pulse now is organized in bars, time signature and accents.


Some notable composers include Johann Sebastian Bach, Georg Friedrich Händel, Claudio Monteverdi and Antonio Vivaldi.

What are we going to learn?

    3.2 – Secular vocal music

    3.3 – Instrumental music

odeNavStructureProperty.value: 1.1. Música monofónica religiosa: el canto gregoriano.

odeComponent.htmlView:
In religious music, the Baroque period introduced new genres, notably the oratorio and the cantata. These genres were used by the various churches (Catholic, Lutheran) as a means of conveying their doctrines.

Oratorys were composed by setting religious stories to music, usually based on texts from the Bible, from both the Old and New Testaments. In oratorys, unlike opera, there is no stage performance; instead, they are simply performed by an orchestra, with choirs and solo singers, who narrate the story on stage without any scenery or action.

The cantata is a musical form written to be sung (unlike the sonata, which is written to be played). It is a vocal work that combines solo singing, choruses and instrumental accompaniment. It is like a miniature opera, but with two key differences: like the oratorio, it has no theatrical performance (there are no sets, costumes or staging), but it is much shorter.

odeNavStructureProperty.value: 1.2. Música monofónica profana: trovadores y troveros

odeComponent.htmlView:
Look at the following image. What sort of musical work is this?

It is clear that this is a theatrical scene set in ancient times, with music playing and people singing. The image is from an opera scene, specifically Handel’s *Julius Caesar*.

Opera is an extremely important genre of vocal music that emerged during this period, and it can be defined as a musical theatre production. The first opera in history is generally considered to be *Orfeo* by the composer Claudio Monteverdi, which premiered in 1607 and is based on the Greek myth of Orpheus and Eurydice.


The structure of a Baroque opera consists mainly of:

  • Overture: an opening instrumental piece that signals to the audience the start of the performance.
  • Recitative: spoken sections in which the singers imitate the natural rhythm of speech to advance the plot.
  • Arias: the lyrical and emotional heart of the work. They pause the dramatic action so that the soloist can express their deepest feelings with a magnificent display of virtuosity.
  • Choruses: pieces in which the choir takes part to represent collective characters.
  • Interludes: instrumental pieces that allowed for scene changes or dances.

odePagStructure.blockName: Instrumental music has gone its own way!

odeComponent.htmlView:
During the Baroque period, instrumental music achieved definitive independence from vocal music. Music was composed specifically for instruments (the refinement of which opened up many possibilities), giving rise to purely instrumental genres such as the concerto, the suite and the fugue.

The concerto

This word probably derives from the Italian term ‘concertare’, which could be translated as ‘to rival, to compete’. This makes sense, as this instrumental genre is based on a certain ‘rivalry’ between different groups of instruments. During the Baroque period, there were two variants of this genre:

Concerto grosso The musical rivalry or dialogue takes place between a small group of instruments, known as the concertino, and the rest of the orchestra, or tutti. Corelli and Handel were particularly notable in this genre. The concerto grosso would disappear by the end of the Baroque period, as the solo concerto came to dominate.
Concerto solo A dialogue is established between a single instrument (sometimes two) and the orchestra. Torelli, Vivaldi and Bach were particularly notable in this regard. The solo concerto has continued to be performed right up to the present day.



It is structured in three parts or movements that contrast in tempo:

PART I: FAST PARTE II: SLOW PARTE III: FAST


The suite

The other major instrumental genre of the Baroque period was the dance suite, or, in other words, a ‘sequence of dances’. The suite consists of several movements that contrast in character. The most common sequence of dances was allemande–courante–sarabande–giga.

  • Allemande: of German origin, in duple metre and of moderate tempo. It has a serious, walking-like character.
  • Courante: of French origin, in triple metre and fast in tempo. It is lively and features leaping movements.
  • Sarabande: of Spanish (and Latin American) origin, with a triple metre and a very slow tempo. It is unhurried, solemn and majestic.
  • Giga: of English/Irish origin, with a fast triple metre (a fast tempo subdivided into three) and a very fast tempo. It is cheerful, energetic and brings the suite to a close.


The fugue

It is a complex, polyphonic musical form based on imitation. It consists of a short melody (called the subject) which is first introduced in one voice and is then copied and pursued by the other voices throughout the entire piece, as in a game of musical hide-and-seek.

odeComponent.htmlView:
As we have seen, the Baroque period saw a great deal of development in instrumental music, in contrast to the dominance of vocal polyphony during the Renaissance. During the Baroque period, instruments reached a high level of perfection and were already being built in a similar way to those of today. It was the era of the great luthiers (instrument makers), such as the Italian Stradivari, whose stringed instruments, known as Stradivarius, are still considered the finest in the world.

The organ

One instrument that underwent significant development during the Baroque period was the organ, an instrument played with great mastery by composers such as Handel and Bach. Spectacular pipe organs were built in churches and cathedrals. This instrument is played using one or more keyboards, the keys of which open valves so that air generated by a bellows causes the pipes to sound; depending on their shape and size, these pipes produce different timbres. These organs also incorporated a pedalboard for playing the lowest notes (basso continuo) with the feet.

The orchestra in the Baroque period

In the Baroque period, largely thanks to the technical perfection achieved by the bowed string instruments (violin, viola, cello and double bass), the concept of the orchestra as we understand it today emerged. During this period, orchestras were smaller in size compared to those of today. They consisted, essentially, of the string section and the harpsichord, a keyboard instrument that provided chordal support for the basso continuo. However, the Baroque orchestra, particularly in its early days, did not have a fixed set of instruments, but often depended on the number of musicians available.

In addition, depending on the composition, the ensemble included woodwind instruments (flute, oboe and bassoon), brass instruments (trumpets and horns) and percussion (timpani). A typical ensemble consisted of around twenty-five musicians. Unlike modern orchestras, the conductor usually conducted whilst seated and playing the harpsichord.
